analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security benefits and funds them by taxing earnings above the payroll-tax cap.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill: it was referred to the Ways and Means Committee on September 8, 2016, sent to its Social Security subcommittee four days later, and died there with 47 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise Social Security benefits for future retirees and disabled workers by changing the benefit formula, switch the annual cost-of-living adjustment to a new index that tracks what retired households actually spend on (especially health care), and lift benefits for widows and widowers in two-income households to at least 75% of what the couple received. To pay for it, the bill would make a share of earnings above the annual Social Security payroll-tax cap subject to Social Security taxes, and would count some of those above-cap earnings toward benefits. It also protects low-income SSI recipients from being pushed down by the benefit increases.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security beneficiaries — retirees, disabled workers, and especially surviving spouses in two-earner couples, whose benefits would rise to at least 75% of the couple's previous amount. Older retirees gain from a cost-of-living index that reflects their higher spending on health care. Lower-earning beneficiaries gain the most from the flat-dollar increase in the benefit formula's first tier.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees, disabled workers, and surviving spouses

how_it_helps.text: The bill raises the first tier of the benefit formula from 90% to 95% of average earnings, phased in from 2021 through 2024, and adds a new 5% tier that counts earnings above the payroll-tax cap toward benefits — both changes raise the initial checks of people who become eligible after 2021.

The bill directs the Bureau of Labor Statistics to publish a new Consumer Price Index for Elderly Consumers and use it for Social Security cost-of-living increases, so adjustments track the spending of retired households rather than the general workforce; seniors typically spend more on health care, which has historically risen faster than the standard index.

The bill sets widow's and widower's benefits at no less than 75% of the combined benefit the couple received before the spouse's death, a group that currently faces steep benefit drops when one partner dies.
The bill holds SSI recipients harmless so that the higher Social Security benefits cannot reduce or eliminate their supplemental income.

analysis.who_pays: High earners and their employers. The bill changes the tax rules so that a share of wages above the annual payroll-tax cap (about $118,500 in 2016) is treated as taxable Social Security wages — the combined 12.4% employee-and-employer tax would apply there, and high-earning self-employed people would pay the same on above-cap business income. In exchange, their above-cap earnings would count modestly toward benefits (5% of the excess).

drawbacks.text: The bill is a direct payroll-tax increase on earnings above the annual cap for high-income workers, their employers, and high-earning self-employed people — opponents argue the 12.4% combined rate on top of existing taxes discourages work and hiring at high-wage firms.

As written, the bill text's tax schedule applies to 80% of above-cap wages in 2017 and steps down to zero by 2021, while the benefit increases are permanent — a mismatch that would leave the expansion without permanent dedicated revenue if taken literally.

The benefit-formula boost applies to every new beneficiary, including affluent retirees; it is not narrowly targeted at those with the least income, and above-cap earners would begin receiving slightly larger benefits from their excess earnings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit changes target real gaps: surviving spouses of two-earner couples take some of the steepest benefit cuts under current law, and seniors' cost of living rises faster than the index now used for adjustments. The funding falls on earnings above the payroll cap, which only top earners reach. The serious flaw is the bill text's own tax schedule, which as written phases out after 2020 while the benefits run forever; a supporter would have to fix that before the bill could honestly be called fiscally balanced.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee and its Social Security subcommittee, which never held a hearing or vote, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Rep. Linda Sánchez introduced the bill on September 8, 2016, late in the second session of the 114th Congress.
It was referred the same day to the House Ways and Means Committee and, in addition, to the Education and the Workforce Committee.

On September 12, 2016, it was referred to the Ways and Means Subcommittee on Social Security, and the record shows no further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
The bill had 47 cosponsors, all of them House Democrats, and no Republican support.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners whose above-cap wages would have faced the new payroll tax, and their employers, are better off because the bill died — current Social Security tax rules and benefit formulas stay exactly as they were.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners above the payroll-tax cap

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 8, 2016, to expand Social Security benefits funded by payroll taxes on earnings above the cap.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Republican signed on.

against.what_they_did: The committee took up the bill only by referral to its Social Security subcommittee and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor vote; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 48 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; Republicans held the House majority and the Ways and Means chairmanship, and the bill received no hearing or vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.industry: High earners above the payroll-tax cap
industries.note: The bill would apply the Social Security payroll tax to a share of wages and self-employment income above the annual cap, a direct cost falling only on the top slice of earners; their cost funds benefit increases for retirees, disabled workers, and survivors.
The employer half of the payroll tax would apply to above-cap wages, raising payroll costs at firms concentrated in high-compensation fields such as finance, technology, and law.
